fetched_contents.text: The Normal Menstrual Cycle and the Control of Ovulation - Endotext ABSTRACT Menstruation is the cyclic, orderly sloughing of the uterine lining, in response to the interactions of hormones produced by the hypothalamus, pituitary, and ovaries. The menstrual cycle may be divided into two phases: (1) follicular or proliferative phase, and (2) the luteal or secretory phase. The length of a menstrual cycle is the number of days between the first day of menstrual bleeding of one cycle to the onset of menses of the next cycle. The median duration of a menstrual cycle is 28 days with most cycle lengths between 25 to 30 days (1-3. Patients who experience menstrual cycles that occur at intervals less than 21 days are termed polymenorrheic, while patients who experience prolonged menstrual cycles greater than 35 days, are termed oligomenorrheic. The typical volume of blood lost during menstruation is approximately 30 mL (4). Any amount greater than 80 mL is considered abnormal (4). The menstrual cycle is typically most irregular around the extremes of reproductive life (menarche and menopause) due to anovulation and inadequate follicular development (5-7). The luteal phase of the cycle is relatively constant in all women, with a duration of 14 days. The variability of cycle length is usually derived from varying lengths of the follicular phase of the cycle, which can range from 10 to 16 days. For complete coverage of this and related topics, please visit www.endotext.org. THE FOLLICULAR PHASE (Fig.1) Figure 1. Hormonal, Ovarian, endometrial, and basal body temperature changes and relations throughout the normal menstrual cycle. (From Carr BR, Wilson JD. Disorders of the ovary and female reproductive tract. In: Braunwald E, Isselbacher KJ, Petersdorf RG, et al, eds. Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine. 11th ed. New York: McGraw-Hill, 1987: 1818-1837. The follicular phase begins from the first day of menses until ovulation. Lower temperatures on a basal body temperature chart, and more importantly, the development of ovarian follicles, characterize this phase. Folliculogenesis begins during the last few days of the preceding menstrual cycle until the release of the mature follicle at ovulation. Declining steroid production by the corpus luteum and the dramatic fall of inhibin A allows for follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) to rise during the last few days of the menstrual cycle (Fig. 2) (8). Another influential factor on the FSH level in the late luteal phase is related to an increase in GnRH pulsatile secretion secondary to a decline in both estradiol and progesterone levels (9). This elevation in FSH allows for the recruitment of a cohort of ovarian follicles in each ovary, one of which is destined to ovulate during the next menstrual cycle. Once menses ensues, FSH levels begin to decline due to the negative feedback of estrogen and the negative effects of inhibin B produced by the developing follicle (Fig. 2) (8, 10-12). FSH activates the aromatase enzyme in granulosa cells, which converts androgens to estrogen. A decline in FSH levels leads to the production of a more androgenic microenvironment within adjacent follicles to the growing dominant follicle. Also, the granulosa cells of the growing follicle secrete a variety of peptides that may play an autocrine/paracrine role in the inhibition of development of the adjacent follicles. Figure 2. Inhibin level changes throughout the menstrual cycle. Inhibin B dominates the follicular phase of the cycle, while Inhibin A dominates the luteal phase. Development of the dominant follicle has been described in three stages: (1) Recruitment, (2) Selection, and (3) Dominance (Fig.3). The recruitment stage takes place during days 1 through 4 of the menstrual cycle. During this stage, FSH leads to recruitment of a cohort of follicles from the pool of non-proliferating follicles. Between cycle days 5 and 7, selection of a follicle takes place whereby only one follicle is selected from the cohort of recruited follicles to ovulate, and the remaining follicles will undergo atresia. Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), a product of granulosa cells, is believed to play a role in the selection of the dominant follicle (13, 14). By cycle day 8, one follicle exerts its dominance by promoting its own growth and suppressing the maturation of the other ovarian follicles thus becoming the dominant follicle. Figure 3. Time course for recruitment, selection, and ovulation of the dominant ovarian follicle (DF) with onset of atresia among other follicles of the cohort (N-1). (From Hodgen GD. The dominant ovarian follicle. Fertil Steril 1982; 38:281-300). During the follicular phase, serum estradiol levels rise in parallel to the growth of follicle size as well as to the increasing number of granulosa cells. FSH receptors exist exclusively on the granulosa cell membranes. Increasing FSH levels during the late luteal phase leads to an increase in the number of FSH receptors and ultimately to an increase in estradiol secretion by granulosa cells. It is important to note that the increase in FSH receptor numbers is due to an increase in the population of granulosa cells and not due to an increase in the concentration of FSH receptors per granulosa cell. Each granulosa cell has approximately 1500 FSH receptors by the secondary stage of follicular development and FSH receptor numbers remains relatively constant for the remainder of development (15). The rise in estradiol secretion appears to increase the total number of estradiol receptors on the granulosa cells (16). fetched_contents.text: Gender and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system Fundam Clin Pharmacol. 2010 Dec;24(6):687-98. doi: 10.1111/j.1472-8206.2010.00854.x. Authors Affiliation * 1 Division of Cardiology, The Jikei University School of Medicine, 3-25-8 Nishi-shimbashi, Minato-ku, Tokyo 105-8461, Japan. * PMID: 20608988 * DOI: 10.1111/j.1472-8206.2010.00854.x Abstract Premenopausal women are protected to some extent from cardiovascular and kidney diseases. Because this protection weakens after menopause, sex hormones are believed to play an important role in the pathogenesis of cardiovascular and kidney diseases. The cardiovascular system and the kidneys are regulated by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), which in turn, appears to be regulated by sex hormones. In general, oestrogen increases angiotensinogen levels and decreases renin levels, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) activity, AT(1) receptor density, and aldosterone production. Oestrogen also activates counterparts of the RAAS such as natriuretic peptides, AT(2) receptor density, and angiotensinogen (1-7). Progesterone competes with aldosterone for mineralocorticoid receptor. Less is known about androgens, but testosterone seems to increase renin levels and ACE activity. These effects of sex hormones on the RAAS can explain at least some of the gender differences in cardiovascular and kidney diseases. fetched_contents.text: Local Renin-Angiotensin System in the Reproductive System Abstract The renin-angiotensin system (RAS) is well known as regulator of electrolytes and blood pressure. Besides this function, there are numerous studies supporting the idea of a local tissue RAS. This system controls the local activity of the different RAS family members, especially of the functional proteins Angiotensin II and Angiotensin (1–7). Those antagonistically acting proteins have been described to be expressed in different organ systems including the human reproductive tract. Therefore, this local RAS has been suspected to be involved in the control and regulation of physiological and pathological conditions in the female reproduction tract. This review of the available literature summarizes the physiological influence of the RAS on the follicular development, ovarian angiogenesis, and placental- and uterine function. In addition, in the second part the role of the RAS concerning ovarian- and endometrial cancer becomes elucidated. This section includes possible novel therapeutic strategies via inhibition of RAS-mediated tumor growth and angiogenesis. Looking at a very complex system of agonistic and antagonistic tissue factors, it may be supposed that the RAS in the female reproduction tract will be of rising scientific interest in the upcoming years. Keywords: endometrial cancer, endometrium, ovarian cancer, ovary, renin-angiotensin system, reproductive tract, local Introduction The Renin-Angiotensin system (RAS) is of paramount importance for the perpetuation of the circular flow, regulating the electrolyte metabolism thus the blood pressure (1–4). This considerable function of the RAS is mediated by the systemic RAS-pathway. The latter consists of a cascade of peptides, acting as precursors which become transformed by different enzymes into the bioactive end products (5). The main protein of this system is Angiotensinogen, which is synthesized in the liver (6). Following the pathway, Angiotensinogen becomes converted into Angiotensin I, catalyzed by Renin, which is of renal origin. Subsequently, Angiotensin I can be further modulated by the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) I to Angiotensin II or by ACE II to Angiotensin (1–9). Angiotensin (1–9) then becomes transformed by ACE or neutral endopeptidase (NEP) into Angiotensin (1–7) (7–9). Those two bioactive effector molecules, Angiotensin II and Angiotensin (1–7) act in an antagonistic way by binding to different receptors: angiotensin receptor type 1 (AT1R) and type 2 (AT2R) or Mas-receptor (10). The G-coupled Mas-receptor mediates vasodilatory and anti-proliferative effects and antagonizes actions of the AT1R (11). In recent years, attention has also focused on the evidence of a widespread local tissue RAS (12). Expression of elements of this local RAS has been described in different parts of the human reproductive tract. Apparently, the both antagonistic bioactive proteins of the RAS, in particular Angiotensin II and Angiotensin (1–7) can result from the local tissue RAS (13, 14). This local production of the bioactive peptides is not necessarily dependent on the local expression of all components of the local tissue RAS, since it is also possible to take up components from the circulation, such as renin. Normal menstrual cycle phases and hormonal changes are best understood as a cyclic sequence driven by ovarian steroid feedback. The follicular phase begins with menses and ends with ovulation, while the luteal phase follows ovulation and is marked by a relatively constant duration of about 14 days [N1-F1]. During the follicular phase, estrogen levels rise in parallel with follicle growth and the increasing number of granulosa cells, whereas progesterone levels are low at cycle onset and remain low until ovulation [N1-F1]. FSH declines after menses because of negative estrogen feedback, and during the late luteal phase, FSH rises again, which helps recruit follicles for the next cycle [N1-F1]. Estrogen also stimulates LH receptor formation on granulosa cells, which can prime the pituitary for LH release and progesterone secretion [N1-F1].

In the luteal phase, progesterone rises sharply after ovulation as the corpus luteum secretes it, while estrogen remains elevated but not as dramatically as progesterone [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that menstrual bleeding and phase transitions affect background physiology: cycle length variability is largely determined by the follicular phase, and the luteal phase is relatively constant in most women [N1-F1]. The transition from follicular to luteal phase involves a sharp drop in estradiol and progesterone, which can elevate FSH and influence follicle recruitment [N1-F1]. In the broader context, cardiovascular and renal physiology change across the menstrual cycle. Studies suggest that systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure decline, followed by compensatory heart rate acceleration, and that menstrual cycle phases are associated with changes in cardiovascular, renal, and hemodynamic parameters [N4-R1], [N4-R4]. This indicates that the menstrual cycle is not just a reproductive event but a dynamic state that alters hemodynamic and renal background physiology [N4-R1], [N4-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a clear phase-dependent hormonal pattern: low estrogen/progesterone at the start of the cycle, rising estrogen during the follicular phase, a sharp rise in progesterone after ovulation, and a relatively stable luteal phase [N1-F1]. Menstrual bleeding and phase transitions matter because they signal hormonal resets and physiological shifts, especially in FSH, estradiol, and progesterone [N1-F1]. Cardiovascular and renal physiology also shift across the cycle, which is important for interpreting any hormone-related changes in women’s physiology [N4-R1], [N4-R4].

Estrogen increases angiotensinogen levels and decreases renin levels, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) activity, AT1 receptor density, and aldosterone production, while also activating RAAS-related natriuretic peptides, AT2 receptor density, and angiotensinogen (1-7) [N3-F3]. Progesterone, by contrast, leads to sodium loss and a compensatory increase in renin secretion, plasma renin activity, angiotensin II (AII), and plasma aldosterone [N3-R5]. These findings indicate that estrogen and progesterone are not merely bystanders but active regulators of RAS output, with estrogen broadly favoring anti-hypertensive and natriuretic effects and progesterone favoring sodium retention and compensatory RAAS activation [N3-F3], [N3-R5].

The evidence also suggests that sex steroids can influence prorenin secretion indirectly through RAS and metabolic pathways. Estrogen status affects multiple RAAS pathways, including angiotensinogen, renin, ACE, and aldosterone biosynthesis [N3-R1]. Progesterone’s effects on sodium balance and AII/aldosterone suggest that it can indirectly alter the need for renin secretion, since renin is the enzyme that initiates the RAS cascade [N3-R5]. In addition, the review of the local RAS in the reproductive system indicates that ovarian steroid receptor expression is relevant to follicular development and that RAS components are expressed in granulosa cells [N5-F2]. This implies that ovarian steroid receptors may mediate the local effects of estrogen and progesterone on RAS signaling, even if the evidence here does not explicitly detail the receptor subtypes or signaling pathways in prorenin regulation [N5-F2].

Overall, the mechanisms are best described as mixed direct and indirect. Estrogen and progesterone directly alter angiotensinogen, renin, ACE, and aldosterone, while also indirectly influencing RAS activity through sodium balance, receptor density, and local ovarian steroid signaling [N3-F3], [N3-R5], [N5-F2]. The direct effects are clearer for estrogen’s inhibition of renin and progesterone’s stimulation of renin and aldosterone, whereas indirect effects involve broader RAS regulation, sodium homeostasis, and local reproductive tissue signaling [N3-R1], [N3-R5], [N5-F2].

## How plasma prorenin varies throughout the normal menstrual cycle

The evidence suggests that plasma prorenin is not constant across the menstrual cycle. Instead, it appears to vary in a phase-dependent manner, with the clearest pattern being an elevation during the luteal phase and a return to baseline during the follicular phase. One source states that circulating RAS components peak when plasma estrogen levels are highest, during the luteal phase of the normal menstrual cycle [N6-R1]. Another source reports that prorenin remained elevated during the mid-luteal phase and returned to baseline during the follicular phase, with a maximum increase averaging 80% [N6-R3]. Together, these findings support a menstrual-cycle pattern in which prorenin rises during the luteal phase and declines during the follicular phase, rather than remaining cyclically constant [N6-R1], [N6-R3].

## What hormonal mechanisms underlie these fluctuations?

The hormonal mechanism appears to be rooted in the interaction between ovarian steroids and the renin-angiotensin system (RAS). Estrogen and progesterone do not act as isolated regulators; they shape RAS activity through both direct and indirect effects.

### 1) Estrogen generally reduces RAS activity
Estrogen increases angiotensinogen levels and decreases renin levels, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) activity, AT1 receptor density, and aldosterone production [N3-F3]. It also activates natriuretic peptides, AT2 receptor density, and angiotensinogen (1-7) [N3-F3]. In other words, estrogen favors a more anti-hypertensive and natriuretic RAS profile, which is consistent with the idea that estrogen can lower circulating RAS drive [N3-F3].

### 2) Progesterone increases RAS activity
Progesterone has the opposite effect. It leads to sodium loss and a compensatory increase in renin secretion, plasma renin activity, angiotensin II (AII), and plasma aldosterone [N3-R5]. This means progesterone can raise RAS output, partly by stimulating renin and aldosterone and partly by altering sodium balance [N3-R5].

### 3) Sex steroids influence prorenin indirectly through broader RAS and metabolic pathways
The evidence also shows that estrogen status affects multiple RAAS pathways, including angiotensinogen, renin, ACE, and aldosterone biosynthesis [N3-R1]. Progesterone’s effects on sodium balance and AII/aldosterone suggest that it can indirectly alter the need for renin secretion, because renin is the enzyme that initiates the RAS cascade [N3-R5]. In addition, the local RAS in the reproductive system indicates that ovarian steroid receptor expression is relevant to follicular development and that RAS components are expressed in granulosa cells [N5-F2]. This implies that ovarian steroid receptors may mediate local RAS signaling and therefore indirectly influence prorenin-related regulation, although the evidence here does not explicitly detail the receptor subtypes or signaling pathways involved [N5-F2].

## How the menstrual cycle phases shape these hormonal effects

The menstrual cycle itself is structured around ovarian steroid feedback. The follicular phase begins with menses and ends with ovulation, while the luteal phase follows ovulation and is marked by a relatively constant duration of about 14 days [N1-F1]. During the follicular phase, estrogen levels rise in parallel with follicle growth and granulosa-cell number, whereas progesterone levels are low at cycle onset and remain low until ovulation [N1-F1]. FSH declines after menses because of negative estrogen feedback, and during the late luteal phase, FSH rises again, which helps recruit follicles for the next cycle [N1-F1].

After ovulation, progesterone rises sharply as the corpus luteum secretes it, while estrogen remains elevated but not as dramatically as progesterone [N1-F1]. This phase transition is important because menstrual bleeding and phase transitions affect background physiology. Cycle length variability is largely determined by the follicular phase, and the luteal phase is relatively constant in most women [N1-F1]. The transition from follicular to luteal phase involves a sharp drop in estradiol and progesterone, which can elevate FSH and influence follicle recruitment [N1-F1].

## How cardiovascular and renal physiology fits into this picture

Prorenin should not be interpreted in isolation. Cardiovascular and renal physiology change across the menstrual cycle. Studies suggest that systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure decline, followed by a compensatory heart rate acceleration, and that menstrual cycle phases are associated with changes in cardiovascular, renal, and hemodynamic parameters [N4-R1], [N4-R4]. This means prorenin is part of a broader hemodynamic and RAS-regulated system rather than a standalone marker [N4-R1], [N4-R4].

Progesterone’s effects on sodium balance and the compensatory increase in renin and aldosterone also show that menstrual-phase changes in RAS can influence blood pressure and fluid homeostasis [N3-R5]. Combined with the local RAS findings, this suggests that ovarian steroids can modulate both systemic and tissue-based RAS activity, which may explain why prorenin changes during the cycle [N5-F2].

## What the evidence says about limitations and interpretation

The evidence for prorenin variation is somewhat limited but suggestive. The clearest direct measurement in the provided evidence is a single study showing elevated mid-luteal prorenin [N6-R3]. Another source reports that circulating RAS components peak during the luteal phase, supporting a phase-dependent pattern [N6-R1]. However, the evidence base is thin: the broader RAS-source excerpt is not itself a prorenin study and therefore cannot be used to infer methodology [N6-R1]. The other sources in this aggregate are general references on prorenin, RAS regulation, or menstrual cycle physiology rather than direct prorenin measurements [N2-R1], [N2-R2], [N2-R4], [N2-R5].

Study limitations are important. The menstrual cycle is inherently variable, especially across reproductive age, with cycle length and variability differing substantially from under 20 to above 50 years old [N6-R4]. This makes phase assignment and comparison difficult unless studies control for cycle timing and individual differences. The evidence also suggests that menstrual-cycle prorenin studies would need to account for background hormonal variation, phase transitions, and other confounders [N6-R1], [N6-R3], [N6-R4].

## Integrated conclusion

Overall, the best-supported conclusion is that plasma prorenin varies during the normal menstrual cycle, with evidence pointing to a luteal-phase peak and a follicular-phase return to baseline [N6-R1], [N6-R3]. The hormonal mechanism is best understood as estrogen reducing RAS activity and progesterone increasing it, with prorenin likely influenced by both direct RAS regulation and indirect steroid effects on sodium balance, receptor density, and local ovarian steroid signaling [N3-F3], [N3-R5], [N5-F2]. Cardiovascular and renal physiology also shift across the cycle, reinforcing that prorenin should be interpreted within the broader context of menstrual-phase hemodynamics and RAS regulation [N4-R1], [N4-R4]. However, the evidence base is limited, so these findings should be treated as suggestive rather than definitive [N6-R1], [N6-R3], [N6-R4].

The evidence also shows that estrogen status affects multiple RAAS pathways, including angiotensinogen, renin, ACE, and aldosterone biosynthesis [N3-R1]. Studies suggest that systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure decline, followed by a compensatory heart rate acceleration, and that menstrual cycle phases are associated with changes in cardiovascular, renal, and hemodynamic parameters [N4-R1], [N4-R4]. This means prorenin is part of a broader hemodynamic and RAS-regulated system rather than a standalone marker [N4-R1], [N4-R4].

Progesterone’s effects on sodium balance and the compensatory increase in renin and aldosterone also show that menstrual-phase changes in RAS can influence blood pressure and fluid homeostasis [N3-R5]. Combined with the local RAS findings, this suggests that ovarian steroids can modulate both systemic and tissue-based RAS activity, which may explain why prorenin changes during the cycle [N5-F2].

## What the evidence says about limitations and interpretation

The evidence for prorenin variation is somewhat limited but suggestive. The clearest direct measurement in the provided evidence is a single study showing elevated mid-luteal prorenin [N6-R3]. Another source reports that circulating RAS components peak during the luteal phase, supporting a phase-dependent pattern [N6-R1]. However, the evidence base is thin: the broader RAS-source excerpt is not itself a prorenin study and therefore cannot be used to infer methodology [N6-R1]. The other sources in this aggregate are general references on prorenin, RAS regulation, or menstrual cycle physiology rather than direct prorenin measurements [N2-R1], [N2-R2], [N2-R4], [N2-R5].

Study limitations are important. The menstrual cycle is inherently variable, especially across reproductive age, with cycle length and variability differing substantially from under 20 to above 50 years old [N6-R4]. This makes phase assignment and comparison difficult unless studies control for cycle timing and individual differences. The evidence also suggests that menstrual-cycle prorenin studies would need to account for background hormonal variation, phase transitions, and other confounders [N6-R1], [N6-R3], [N6-R4].

## Integrated conclusion

Overall, the best-supported conclusion is that plasma prorenin varies during the normal menstrual cycle, with evidence pointing to a luteal-phase peak and a follicular-phase return to baseline [N6-R1], [N6-R3]. The hormonal mechanism is best understood as estrogen reducing RAS activity and progesterone increasing it, with prorenin likely influenced by both direct RAS regulation and indirect steroid effects on sodium balance, receptor density, and local ovarian steroid signaling [N3-F3], [N3-R5], [N5-F2]. Cardiovascular and renal physiology also shift across the cycle, reinforcing that prorenin should be interpreted within the broader context of menstrual-phase hemodynamics and RAS regulation [N4-R1], [N4-R4]. However, the evidence base is limited, so these findings should be treated as suggestive rather than definitive [N6-R1], [N6-R3], [N6-R4].
